1.caption: Fig. 1. The tetrahedron of affinities: the four corners are the four pure elements, and the points lie a sixth apart (only the edges, and the points upon the faces, are drawn; a cross marks a point whose frame is null, an open circle an empty cell). Taking fire less water across and air less earth upward, and so casting the tetrahedron upon a plane, gives the table of Fig. 2

2.caption: Fig. 2. The table of elemental affinities. Across, fire less water; upward, air less earth; in each cell the affinities of the points it holds (fire, water, air, earth, in sixths). The filled cells have all been found as natural crystals; the crossed cell in the middle has a null frame and can form no crystal; the four open cells at the middles of the sides are the empty cells, whose bias passes the bound an ordinary place can bear

3.caption: Fig. 3. The greatest crystal seen (inches) falls as the number of bias grows (filled points); the straight line drawn through the six comes to nothing at some eight and a half. The upright dotted line is the bound found by the trials of added bias in Table III, the thin lines beside it the least and greatest totals of the twenty-one pieces; the open point at the far right is the number of bias of the empty cells, nine
